thread.title: Ciena and 3 Other Stocks That Would Gain From a Huawei Ban - Barron's

title: Ciena and 3 Other Stocks That Would Gain From a Huawei Ban - Barron's
text:
4 Stocks That Would Benefit From a U.S. Ban Against China’s Huawei By Jan. 29, 2019 1:43 p.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Qilai Shen/Bloomberg Text size
After the U.S. Department of Justice unveiled charges against Huawei Technologies on Monday, some analysts have begun to explore the possibility that the Chinese telecom giant will be barred from doing business with American companies.
The charges include accusations that smartphone and network equipment maker Huawei violated U.S. sanctions on Iran, and that it stole trade secrets from T-Mobile US (TMUS) . The U.S. also formally requested that Huawei Chief Financial Officer Meng Wanzhou be extradited from Canada .
MKM Partners managing director Michael Genovese thinks that it is now more likely than not that Huawei will eventually be entirely cut off from purchasing U.S. components. That’s bad news for its suppliers in the optical-components market, which provide integral parts in the fiber-optic network infrastructure that Huawei produces. Genovese estimates that Huawei is responsible for about 15% of the industry’s revenue.
Stocks of several U.S. companies in the space have fallen since the DoJ announcement. San Jose, Ca.-based NeoPhotonics (NPTN) is the most exposed, with Huawei responsible for more than 40% of its sales. The stock fell 2.4% on Monday, followed by a 2.4% drop on Tuesday morning. Two other U.S.-based suppliers, with about 15% Huawei exposure each, both slid as well: Lumentum Holdings (LITE) fell 3.5% Monday and another 3.5% Tuesday, while II-VI (IIVI) dropped 1.5% and 1.3%, respectively, on those two days.
Lumentum could be further exposed to Huawei as a potential customer in its 3-D sensing business , which builds the sensors in smartphone systems such as Apple ’s (AAPL) Face ID. Such technology could be used in an upcoming Huawei handset model, as well.
If Huawei is blocked from buying from U.S. companies, the drop-off in sales for optical-component suppliers could be even more severe given that several Chinese makers of telecom equipment are now apparently pre-ordering extra inventory in anticipation of such a move.
“According to our checks, Huawei, ZTE, and FiberHome are currently building optical-component inventory,” Genovese wrote in a report published Tuesday morning. “While near-term results for the industry are likely to be upbeat, investors are unlikely to give much credit unless and until Huawei is explicitly not banned by the U.S. as part of a trade agreement and/or DOJ settlement.”
The charges against Huawei come at a time when global telecom capital spending is ramping up as wireless networks move to 5G, broadband moves to 10G, and fiber-optic networks are upgraded. Taking Huawei out of the market would provide a boost to Western companies that make comparable products that are often more expensive. These competitors include Adtran (ADTN)–up over 4% since Monday’s open–and Nokia (NOK), Ericsson (ERIC), and Ciena (CIEN), the three of which are about flat this week.
5G spending decisions over the coming year could help the Scandinavian telecom-equipment makers gain market share from Huawei, according to Genovese: “We expect Nokia and Ericsson are likely to gain share in South Korea and Japan at Huawei’s expense in 2019, and to gain share significant share in Europe in 2020 as 5G begins to sweep across the continent.”
And with Huawei providing equipment for Chinese 5G networks, cutting it off from key suppliers could naturally stall progress. Genovese no longer believes that China will be able to build a nationwide 5G network in 2019, falling behind South Korea and Japan. A ban could also make a dent in European 5G ambitions, however. European carrier Deutsche Telecom recently warned that cutting out Huawei would delay 5G rollout on the continent by as much as two years.
Huawei is privately held and not listed on any public stock exchange.
